examples.problem_statement: Problem 13. Two cars, P and Q, are travelling towards the junction of two roads which are at right angles to one another. Car P has a velocity of 45 km/h due east and car Q a velocity of 55 km/h due south. Calculate (a) the velocity of car P relative to car Q and (b) the velocity of car Q relative to car P

solution.description: Set up axes before writing any vectors: east is the positive x-direction and north the positive y-direction. Car P's 45 km/h due east becomes 45 in the i-direction, and car Q's 55 km/h due south becomes minus 55 in the j-direction.

solution.operation: Find velocity of P relative to Q
solution.description: The velocity of P relative to Q is the vector difference v_P minus v_Q. Subtracting the negative j-component turns it positive, leaving 45 in the i-direction and 55 in the j-direction.
The two components of that difference are perpendicular, so Pythagoras gives its size: the square root of 2025 plus 3025, which is about 71.06 km/h.
Both components are positive, so the vector points into the north-east quadrant. Its bearing is the arctangent of 55 over 45, about 50.71 degrees measured from east towards north.

solution.operation: Find velocity of Q relative to P
solution.description: Now reverse the reference frame for part (b). The difference v_Q minus v_P is exactly the negative of the vector found in step 2, so both components change sign.

solution.operation: Calculate magnitude and direction for Q relative to P
solution.description: Because that vector is simply the reverse of the earlier one, its magnitude is unchanged at 71.06 km/h while its direction turns through 180 degrees, giving 230.71 degrees, the same as 50.71 degrees south of west.

examples.answer: Velocity of car P relative to car Q is 71.06 km/h at 50.71° north of east. Velocity of car Q relative to car P is 71.06 km/h at 230.71° (or equivalently, 50.71° south of west).

examples.problem_statement: Two cars, P and Q, are travelling towards the junction of two roads which are at right angles to one another. Car P has a velocity of 45 km/h due east and car Q a velocity of 55 km/h due south. Calculate (a) the velocity of car P relative to car Q and (b) the velocity of car Q relative to car P

solution.description: Sketch the space diagram first: the two roads meet at right angles, with P approaching the junction heading east and Q approaching it heading south.
For part (a), draw the velocity diagram by setting the 45 km/h and 55 km/h phasors head to tail, so that the closing side of the figure stands for the velocity of P relative to Q.
Measure that closing side and the angle it makes with the horizontal to get the relative speed and its bearing, 71.06 km/h at 50.71 degrees.
For part (b), redraw the diagram with the reference reversed, so the closing side now runs the other way and stands for the velocity of Q relative to P.

examples.answer: (a) 71.06 km/h at 50.71°; (b) 71.06 km/h in the opposite direction to (a).

concept.technique_name: vector addition and subtraction in i, j, k form

solution.description: Read the two vectors off the question in i, j, k component form, so the subtraction can be handled one component at a time.
Write down the required difference, keeping the second vector in brackets so that the minus sign will be applied to all three of its components.
Remove the brackets by distributing the minus sign, which flips the sign of every component of the second vector: minus 4i, plus 3j, minus 2k.
Gather the i terms together, the j terms together and the k terms together so their coefficients can be combined.
Do the arithmetic inside each group: 3 minus 4 gives minus 1, 2 plus 3 gives 5, and 2 minus 2 gives 0.
The k term is zero and can be dropped, leaving the tidy answer minus i plus 5j.

examples.problem_statement: Given p = 3i + 2k, q = 4i - 2j + 3k and r = -3i + 5j - 4k, determine (a) -r (b) 3p (c) 2p + 3q (d) -p + 2r (e) 0.2p + 0.6q - 3.2r

solution.description: Substitute p, q and r into each of the five expressions and carry out the scalar multiplications first, multiplying every component of a vector by its scalar; for instance minus r flips all three signs of r, and 3p triples each component of p.
Then combine the scaled vectors by adding or subtracting matching i, j and k components separately, which yields each of the answers from (a) to (e).

solution.description: Read the fraction as a division: seven eighths means 7 divided by 8, and that is the division the rest of the steps carry out.
Write 7 as 7.000 under the division bracket. Eight will not go into 7, so the added decimal point and zeros give places to work into.
Eight into 70 goes 8 times, because 8 times 8 is 64, the largest multiple of 8 below 70, and that leaves a remainder of 6.
Bring the next zero down alongside the remainder 6 to make 60, ready for the next division.
Eight into 60 goes 7 times, since 8 times 7 is 56, leaving a remainder of 4.
Bring the next zero down alongside the remainder 4 to make 40.
Eight into 40 goes exactly 5 times with nothing left over, so the division terminates here.
Read the quotient digits 8, 7 and 5 in the order they were found, after the decimal point, to give 0.875.

solution.operation: 16 into 13 will not go. Place the 0 above the 3.
solution.description: Start on the fraction part, thirteen sixteenths. Sixteen will not go into 13, so a zero is placed above the 3 before any decimal digits are found.

solution.operation: Place the decimal point above the decimal point of 13.0000
solution.description: Line the decimal point of the answer up with the decimal point of 13.0000, so every digit that follows lands in its correct place.

solution.operation: 16 into 130 goes 8, remainder 2. Place the 8 above the first zero after the decimal point and carry the 2 remainder to the next digit on the right, making it 20.
solution.description: Bring the first zero down to make 130. Sixteen into 130 goes 8 with remainder 2, so 8 is the first decimal digit and the 2 carries across to make 20.

solution.operation: 16 into 20 goes 1, remainder 4. Place the 1 above the next zero and carry the 4 remainder to the next digit on the right, making it 40.
solution.description: Sixteen into 20 goes 1 with remainder 4, giving the second decimal digit and carrying 4 across to make 40.

solution.operation: 16 into 40 goes 2, remainder 8. Place the 2 above the next zero and carry the 8 remainder to the next digit on the right, making it 80.
solution.description: Sixteen into 40 goes 2 with remainder 8, giving the third decimal digit and carrying 8 across to make 80.

solution.operation: 16 into 80 goes 5, remainder 0. Place the 5 above the next zero.
solution.description: Sixteen into 80 goes 5 exactly, giving the fourth decimal digit and ending the division with no remainder.
The fraction part is therefore 0.8125, so putting the whole number 5 back in front gives 5.8125.

common_mistakes: Stopping after the first division and writing 7 divided by 8 as 0.8, instead of continuing until the remainder is zero.
Converting only the fraction part of the mixed number and giving 0.8125 as the final answer, losing the whole number 5.

concept.technique_name: combining a sine and a cosine into a single sinusoid

examples.problem_statement: Plot the graph of y1 = 3 sin A from A = 0° to A = 360°. On the same axes plot y2 = 2 cos A. By adding ordinates, plot yR = 3 sin A + 2 cos A and obtain a sinusoidal expression for this resultant waveform

solution.operation: Express the sum as a single sine function
solution.description: The aim is to replace the sum of a sine and a cosine of the same angle by one sine wave, so write 3 sin A plus 2 cos A as R sin of A plus alpha, with the amplitude R and phase alpha still to be found.
Expand that single sine using the compound-angle formula, which splits it into a term in sin A and a term in cos A whose coefficients can be compared with the original expression.
Match the coefficients of the two expressions: the sin A terms give R cos alpha equal to 3, and the cos A terms give R sin alpha equal to 2.
Square and add those two matched equations. Since sin squared plus cos squared is 1, alpha drops out and R squared is 9 plus 4, so R is the square root of 13, about 3.606.
Divide the two matched equations instead and R drops out, leaving tan alpha equal to 2 over 3, so alpha is about 33.7 degrees.
Put the amplitude and phase back into the single sine form to give the resultant waveform, root 13 sin of A plus 33.7 degrees, or 3.606 sin of A plus 33.7 degrees.

examples.problem_statement: Given y₁ = 4 sin ωt and y₂ = 3 sin(ωt − π/3), find the resultant yᵣ = y₁ + y₂ by drawing.

solution.description: Note the two waveforms to be added: y1 has amplitude 4 with no phase shift, and y2 has amplitude 3 lagging by pi over 3 radians. They share a frequency, so they can be combined as phasors.
Draw y1 as a horizontal phasor 4 units long, taken as the reference, and y2 as a phasor 3 units long turned 60 degrees below it, since pi over 3 radians is 60 degrees and the shift is negative.

Resolve each phasor into horizontal and vertical parts. The reference phasor gives 4 and 0; the lagging phasor gives 3 cos of minus 60 degrees, which is 1.5, and 3 sin of minus 60 degrees, which is minus 2.598.
Add horizontal to horizontal and vertical to vertical, so the resultant has a horizontal part of 5.5 and a vertical part of minus 2.598.
Those two resultant parts are perpendicular, so Pythagoras gives the resultant amplitude: the square root of 30.25 plus 6.75, about 6.08.
The phase of the resultant is the arctangent of minus 2.598 over 5.5, about minus 25.3 degrees, which is minus 0.44 radians. The negative sign shows the resultant lags the reference.
Write the resultant back as a single sine wave, using the amplitude read off the drawing, 6, and the phase angle of minus 0.44 radians.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: Phasor addition by drawing requires accurate scaling and angle measurement.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Phase angles must be correctly interpreted as leading or lagging.'}
{'point': 'Tip: Use protractor and ruler for precise results.'}
{'point': 'Prerequisite: Understanding of sine waves and phase shifts.'}

Adding the amplitudes to get 7, which ignores the 60 degree phase difference between the two waves.
Dropping the minus sign on the vertical component, so the resultant is reported as leading the reference instead of lagging it.

concept.technique_name: phasor addition and subtraction of sinusoids

examples.problem_statement: Two alternating currents are given by $i_1 = 20 \sin \omega t$ amperes and $i_2 = 10 \sin (\omega t + \pi/3)$ amperes. Determine $i_1 + i_2$ by drawing phasors.

solution.description: Write each current as a phasor. The first has amplitude 20 at 0 degrees and is taken as the reference; the second has amplitude 10 at plus 60 degrees, since a shift of pi over 3 radians leads by 60 degrees.

solution.result: \begin{aligned}i_1 = 20(\cos 0^\circ + j\sin 0^\circ) = 20 + j0 \\ i_2 = 10(\cos 60^\circ + j\sin 60^\circ) = 10(0.5 + j0.866) = 5 + j8.66\end{aligned}
solution.description: Convert both phasors from polar to rectangular form so that their parts can be added. The reference gives 20 horizontally and nothing vertically; the second gives 5 horizontally and 8.66 vertically.
Add the horizontal parts to each other and the vertical parts to each other, giving a resultant of 25 horizontally and 8.66 vertically.
Those parts are at right angles, so Pythagoras gives the resultant amplitude: the square root of 625 plus 75, about 26.46 amperes.
The phase of the resultant is the arctangent of 8.66 over 25, about 19.1 degrees. It is positive, so the resultant leads the reference current.
Return the resultant to time-domain form using the amplitude and phase just found, giving 26.5 sin of omega t plus 19.1 degrees amperes.

examples.problem_statement: For the currents in Problem 5, determine i1 − i2 by drawing phasors

solution.description: Begin the subtraction diagram by drawing the first current, 20 units long, horizontally as the reference phasor.
Add the second current, 10 units long, at 60 degrees leading, drawn as a broken line because it is the phasor that will be reversed.
Subtract by turning that broken phasor through 180 degrees and adding the reversed phasor to the reference head to tail.
The resultant is the phasor drawn from the origin to the tip of the reversed phasor, closing the construction.
Measure the length and angle of that resultant with ruler and protractor, which gives 17 amperes lagging by 0.52 radians.

examples.problem_statement: Determine the resultant of y1 = 5 sin ωt and y2 = 4 sin(ωt − π/6) using the cosine rule.

solution.description: Represent the first wave as a phasor of length 5 at 0 degrees and the second as a phasor of length 4 lagging by pi over 6, that is 30 degrees.
Set the two phasors head to tail so they close a triangle whose third side is the resultant. The angle enclosed between the sides of length 5 and 4 in that triangle is 150 degrees.

Apply the cosine rule to that triangle: the resultant squared is 25 plus 16 minus twice 5 times 4 times cos 150 degrees. Because cos 150 degrees is negative, the subtracted term adds 34.641, giving 75.641.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: Phasor diagrams must be drawn to scale using a ruler and protractor for accurate measurement of magnitude and phase.'}
{'point': 'Caution: When subtracting phasors, always reverse the direction of the phasor being subtracted before adding.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Use known angles like 30°, 60°, 90° for quick construction.'}
{'point': 'Note: The cosine rule can be applied to non-right triangles formed by phasor addition to find exact magnitudes without drawing.'}
common_mistakes: Forgetting to reverse the second phasor before adding when finding i1 minus i2, which returns the sum of about 26.5 amperes instead of 17 amperes.
Using 30 degrees rather than 150 degrees as the angle enclosed by the sides of 5 and 4 in the cosine rule triangle.
Mixing units by entering a phase given in radians, such as pi over 3, into a calculator left in degree mode.

concept.technique_name: resultant of two sinusoids by calculation

examples.problem_statement: Given $ y_1 = 2 \sin \omega t $ and $ y_2 = 3 \sin(\omega t + \pi/4) $, obtain an expression, by calculation, for the resultant, $ y_R = y_1 + y_2 $

solution.description: Note the two waveforms to be added: the first has amplitude 2 with no phase shift, the second amplitude 3 leading by pi over 4 radians.

solution.result: \begin{aligned}y_R = y_1 + y_2 = R\sin(\omega t + \phi) \\ R = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\delta} \\ \phi = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{A_2\sin\delta}{A_1 + A_2\cos\delta}\right)\end{aligned}
solution.description: Because both have the same frequency, their sum is another sine wave of that frequency. Record the standard results for its amplitude and phase in terms of the two amplitudes and the phase difference between them.
Substitute the given values into the amplitude formula: amplitudes 2 and 3, with a phase difference of 45 degrees, which is pi over 4 radians.
Work that amplitude out numerically. Twelve times cos 45 degrees is 8.485, so the amplitude is the square root of 21.485, which is 4.635.
Substitute the same values into the phase formula, which reduces to the arctangent of 2.121 over 4.121.
Evaluate that arctangent. The ratio is 0.5147, so the phase of the resultant is 0.475 radians.
Put the amplitude and phase together to give the resultant as a single sine wave, 4.635 sin of omega t plus 0.475.

common_mistakes: Adding the amplitudes to get 5 instead of using the cosine formula, which gives 4.635.
Leaving the calculator in degree mode at the last step, so the phase is reported as about 27.2 rather than 0.475 radians.

concept.technique_name: phasor addition by horizontal and vertical components

examples.problem_statement: Two alternating voltages are given by $ v_1 = 15 \sin \omega t $ volts and $ v_2 = 25 \sin (\omega t - \pi/6) $ volts. Determine a sinusoidal expression for the resultant $ v_R = v_1 + v_2 $ by finding horizontal and vertical components.

solution.description: Note the two voltages to be added: the first has amplitude 15 and is taken as the reference, the second has amplitude 25 and lags by pi over 6 radians. Same frequency, so their components can be added.

solution.operation: Convert to rectangular form using phasors
solution.result: \begin{aligned}v_1 = 15 \sin \omega t \\ H_1 = 15 \cos 0^\circ = 15 \\ V_1 = 15 \sin 0^\circ = 0 \\ v_2 = 25 \sin (\omega t - \pi/6) \\ H_2 = 25 \cos (-30^\circ) = 25 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 21.65 \\ V_2 = 25 \sin (-30^\circ) = 25 \times (-0.5) = -12.5\end{aligned}
solution.description: Resolve each voltage phasor into a horizontal part, using cosine, and a vertical part, using sine. The reference at 0 degrees gives 15 and 0; the second at minus 30 degrees gives 21.65 and minus 12.5.
Add the horizontal parts to each other and the vertical parts to each other, giving totals of 36.65 volts horizontally and minus 12.5 volts vertically.
Those two totals are at right angles, so Pythagoras combines them into the amplitude of the resultant: the square root of 1499.47, about 38.97 volts.
The phase of the resultant is the arctangent of minus 12.5 over 36.65, about minus 0.33 radians. The minus sign shows the resultant lags the reference voltage.
Write the resultant as a single sine wave using the amplitude and phase just found, 38.97 sin of omega t minus 0.33 volts.

examples.problem_statement:
Data are obtained on the topics given below. State whether they are discrete or continuous data.
(a) The number of days on which rain falls in a month for each month of the year.
(b) The mileage travelled by each of a number of salesmen.
(c) The time that each of a batch of similar batteries lasts.
(d) The amount of money spent by each of several families on food.

solution.operation: Analyze part (a): The number of days on which rain falls in a given month must be an integer value and is obtained by counting the number of days.
solution.description: Take part (a) first. The number of days on which rain falls is found by counting days, so it can only ever come out as a whole number.

solution.operation: Conclude for part (a): These data are discrete.
solution.description: Because counting produces separate whole-number values with nothing possible in between, the rainfall data in part (a) are discrete.

solution.operation: Analyze part (b): A salesman can travel any number of miles (and parts of a mile) between certain limits and these data are measured.
solution.description: Turn to part (b). Mileage is measured rather than counted, and a salesman can cover any distance, including parts of a mile, between the limits.

solution.operation: Conclude for part (b): These data are continuous.
solution.description: Since any value in that range is possible, with no gaps, the mileage data in part (b) are continuous.

solution.operation: Analyze part (c): The time that a battery lasts is measured and can have any value between certain limits.
solution.description: Part (c) works the same way. The life of a battery is a measured time and can take any value between certain limits.

solution.operation: Conclude for part (c): These data are continuous.
solution.description: A measured time has no gaps between its possible values, so the battery data in part (c) are continuous.

solution.operation: Analyze part (d): The amount of money spent on food can only be expressed correct to the nearest pence, the amount being counted.
solution.description: Part (d) looks like a measurement but is not. Money spent on food can only be given to the nearest penny, so the amount is counted in fixed units.

solution.operation: Conclude for part (d): These data are discrete.
solution.description: Because the possible amounts step in fixed units of a penny, the spending data in part (d) are discrete.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: Discrete data come from counting and are whole numbers.'}
{'point': 'Continuous data come from measurement and can be any value within a range.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Money is often treated as discrete because it is counted in fixed units (like pence), even if it seems like a measurement.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Ask yourself — can this be counted exactly (discrete) or measured with infinite precision (continuous)?'}
common_mistakes: Calling the money in part (d) continuous because spending feels like a measurement, when it is counted to the nearest penny and so is discrete.
Deciding by how large or how tidy the numbers look, rather than by whether the quantity is counted or measured.
